text.content: This chapter details the rules for creating and playing droid characters.

Droids are fundamentally different from organic characters. Every droid automatically possesses the Droid Machine/Construct Baseline and operates on a Power Point (PP) system.

Power Points (PP)

A standard droid has a base capacity of 100 Power Points (PP). Because of their mechanical nature, droids do not possess Endurance Points (EP) or Force Points (FP).

  • Consumption: 1 PP/hour for normal operation; 1 PP/minute for strenuous activity (e.g., combat).
  • Low Power (20 PP): The droid receives a visual/auditory low-power warning.
  • Critical Power (10 PP): The droid suffers -1 to DX and IQ.
  • Shutdown (0 PP): The droid shuts down completely. The droid may attempt an IQ-2 roll to perform one final action before going completely inert.

Droid Machine/Construct Baseline

Droid Machine/Construct Baseline

AdvantagesMachine [25 CP]Immunity to poisons, diseases, and metabolic hazards. Does not eat, sleep, or breathe.
AdvantagesInjury Tolerance [20 CP](Unaliving) (Reduced damage multipliers from piercing/impaling weapons).

DisadvantagesUnhealing (Total) [-30 CP]Must be physically repaired; does not heal naturally over time.

Droids can purchase many standard advantages using CP, but some are particularly common:

  • Absolute Timing [2 Points]
  • Description: Your internal chronometer is flawless. You always know exactly what time it is, and you can measure elapsed time down to the fraction of a second.
  • Damage Resistance (DR) [5 points/level]
  • Description: Your chassis is armored. You subtract your DR level from the damage of any physical or energy attack before it affects your Hit Points. For droids, this represents reinforced plating or a hardened chassis.
  • Digital Mind [5 Points]
  • Immune to organic telepathy and Force Mind Tricks -- and to Force Fear, Mnemotherapy, Qâzoi Kyantuska and Summon Fear, which all need an organic mind to work on (see The Force and Droid Minds, @UUID[Compendium.shadowbase.handbook.JournalEntry.cvf2pB6RpI78AvBt]{Chapter 8}). Susceptible to computer slicing (@UUID[Compendium.shadowbase.handbook.JournalEntry.aHFgSZUXNODEwQd2]{Chapter 3}), which is the ordinary way into a droid and needs no Force at all, and to Mechu-deru (@UUID[Compendium.shadowbase.handbook.JournalEntry.cvf2pB6RpI78AvBt]{Chapter 8}), the one Force power that reaches a droid's systems directly. Force Illusion also works, since it feeds false images to optics rather than suggestions to a mind.
  • Doesn’t Breathe [20 Points]
  • Description: You do not require oxygen to function. You are completely immune to inhaled toxins, poison gases, and strangulation, and you can operate freely in a vacuum or underwater.
  • Enhanced Move [20 Points/level]
  • Description: You are built for speed. This doubles your top speed in one specific environment (most commonly Ground for wheeled or tracked droids, or Air for repulsorlift models).
  • Extra Arms [10 Points/arm]
  • Description: You possess more than the standard two manipulator appendages. This allows you to hold multiple items, perform complex multi-handed tasks, and gain bonuses in close-combat grappling.
  • Gizmos [5 Points/gadget]
  • Description: Your chassis is packed with hidden tools and compartments. Once per game session per level of this advantage, you can instantly produce a minor, unspecified tool or gadget perfectly suited to the situation.
  • Injury Tolerance (Unaliving) [20 points]
  • Description: Reduced damage multipliers from piercing and impaling weapons.
  • Machine [25 Points]
  • Description: The defining trait of a mechanical construct. This is a meta-trait that grants you a mechanical body with no biological needs: Immunity to Metabolic Hazards (poisons, diseases, etc.) and a 100-Hour Energy Reserve (non-combat). A machine body cannot heal on its own; that is priced separately as Unhealing (Total) in the droid baseline.
  • Nictitating Membrane [1 Point/level]
  • Description: You have a protective layer over your optical sensors. Each level provides your eyes with Damage Resistance and gives a bonus to resist blinding effects or eye damage.
  • Reputation [Varies, typically 1 to 20 Points]
  • Description: Your specific droid model—or your personal exploits—are well known for something positive (e.g., exceptional reliability, combat prowess, or a famous former owner). This provides a reaction bonus from certain groups of people who recognize you.
  • Calculating Cost: Start with a base of 5 points per +1 reaction bonus (maximum +4). Multiply this by the size of the group affected: Everyone (x1), Large Class like all spacers or all military (x1/2), or Small Class like a specific smuggler ring (x1/3). Finally, multiply by how often you are recognized: All the time (x1), Sometimes/roll of 10 or less (x1/2), or Occasionally/roll of 7 or less (x1/3). Round fractions up.
  • Suggestion (3 Points): A highly reliable T3-series astromech model. +2 Reaction (10 points), recognized by a Large Class of starship mechanics and pilots (x1/2), recognized Sometimes (x1/2).
  • Suggestion (10 Points): A legendary gladiator droid, a droid owned/ associated with a person of some renown, etc. +4 Reaction (20 points), recognized by Everyone (x1), recognized Sometimes (x1/2).
  • Sealed [15 Points]
  • Description: Your internal systems are completely sealed off from the outside world. You are immune to corrosive atmospheres, contact poisons, and extreme environmental pressure or vacuum leaks.

Droids have unique disadvantages reflecting their mechanical nature, they return CP to the character for each taken:

  • Automaton [-15 Points]
  • Description: You are a rigid thinker bound by programming. This meta-trait includes Hidebound, Incurious, and Low Empathy. You do not experience normal emotions, you struggle to understand sapient behavior, and you cannot think “outside the box.”
  • Cannot Learn [-30 Points]
  • Description: You are entirely limited to your factory programming. You cannot spend Character Points to acquire new skills or improve existing ones through experience. Your only way to “learn” is to have new software installed.
  • Electrical [-20 Points]
  • Description: You are vulnerable to power surges. Ion weapons, electromagnetic pulses (EMP), and raw electricity bypass your normal defenses and can short-circuit your systems or shut you down completely.
  • Scheduled Maintenance [-2 to -10 Points]
  • Description: Your complex internal workings require regular upkeep. You must receive periodic maintenance from someone with the appropriate Repair or Mechanic skill, or you will begin to suffer system failures and lose Hit Points. The point value depends on how often you need maintenance and how many people it takes to perform it.
  • No Manipulators [-50 Points]
  • Description: You lack hands or any equivalent appendages. You cannot use weapons, operate standard terminals, or perform tasks requiring fine motor skills (common for astromech or courier droids).
  • Reputation [Varies, typically -1 to -20 Points ]
  • Description: Your specific droid model—or your personal exploits—are infamously known for something negative (e.g., terrifying assassin programming, notorious glitches, or a habit of getting owners killed). This provides a reaction penalty from certain groups of people who recognize you.
  • Calculating Cost: Start with a base of -5 points per -1 reaction penalty (maximum -4). Apply the exact same multipliers for “Group Size” and “Frequency of Recognition” as the positive Reputation advantage (see above).
  • Suggestion (-2 Points): An older protocol droid model notorious for blurting out its owner’s secrets. -2 Reaction (-10 points), recognized by a Large Class of diplomats and merchants (x1/2), recognized Occasionally (x1/3, rounded up to the nearest whole point).
  • Suggestion (-10 Points): An HK-series assassin droid. -4 Reaction (-20 points), recognized by Everyone (x1), recognized Sometimes (x1/2).
  • Reprogrammable [-10 Points]
  • Description: Your mind is purely software. Anyone who captures you and possesses the right skills and equipment can alter your loyalties, erase your memories, or change your core directives against your will.
  • Social Stigma (Valuable Property) [-10 Points]
  • Description: In the eyes of the law, you are an object, not a person. You have no legal rights, you cannot own property, and you are expected to obey the commands of your owner without question.
  • Unhealing (Total) [-30 points]
  • Description: Must be physically repaired; does not heal naturally over time.

Droid Quirks

  • Droidspeak (now a language): Droidspeak is a language now, not a quirk -- see Language (Droidspeak), @UUID[Compendium.shadowbase.handbook.JournalEntry.aHFgSZUXNODEwQd2]{Chapter 3}. Every droid speaks Droidspeak (binary) natively and understands Basic; only vocabulator-equipped models -- protocol droids, HK units, the public-facing patrol droid -- also speak Basic aloud (a linguistic-processor droid speaks a large array of languages besides). A droid that speaks only binary carries Basic at Comprehension-only [0]. No organic can ever speak binary, only understand it.

More than mere tools, droids are complex, modular machines customized to an astounding degree. A character with the Engineer (Droids) skill can build a droid from scratch, repair critical damage, or heavily modify an existing unit. Because droids are built component-by-component, you cannot simply bolt an upgrade onto a general “chassis” without determining the exact mechanical body parts that will house it.

Droid Roles

Players can interact with droids in two distinct ways:

  • Playing as a Droid (CP): During character creation, a player uses Character Points (CP) to buy their entire starting loadout, purchasing a base chassis and immediately augmenting it with better parts. Once the campaign begins, a player-character droid cannot “train” to increase physical attributes. Instead, you must purchase, scavenge, or invent new hardware using Galactic Credits (CR) to upgrade your physical stats mid-campaign.
  • Purchasing a Droid (CR): Organic characters can purchase droids as property, crewmates, or bodyguards using CR. Equipment tables provide both the CP and CR costs for every chassis, processor, and physical component to accommodate both playstyles.

Module Capacity and Slots

Every chassis has a specific capacity for upgrades, broken down into distinct categories. Understanding how these slots interact is crucial to maximizing your droid’s efficiency before assembly begins:

  • Power Core Slot: Every chassis possesses exactly one primary Power Core slot. This dictates the maximum Power Point pool and is strictly required for the droid to function.
  • Actuator Slots: Dedicated to the physical drive systems, servos, and hydraulic motors. Modifying or upgrading items in these slots directly impacts the droid’s Strength and lifting capacity.
  • Reflex Wiring Slots: The housing for the droid’s fiber-optic nervous system and kinetic processors. Upgrades placed in these slots dictate manual dexterity, Dexterity, and reaction times.
  • Core Upgrades: These represent stripping out the factory-standard skeleton or central architecture and replacing it with superior parts. Because they replace the fundamental body rather than bolting onto it, Core upgrades do not consume standard module slots. A droid may have one upgrade from every Core category installed simultaneously, but cannot stack multiple upgrades from the same category.
  • Internal Slots: These represent the available physical space and processing ports located inside the chassis. They are used for sensory suites, communication arrays, concealed compartments, and internal hardware. Items in these slots are protected by the droid’s outer armor.
  • External Slots: These are structural hardpoints bolted onto the outside of the chassis, dedicated to heavy, bulky, or combat-oriented modifications. Examples include heavy armor plating, integrated weapon mounts, and specialized locomotion upgrades.
  • Utility Slots: Dedicated hardpoints for specialized vocational gear, built-in tools, astromech scomp links, or medical dispensers. These are typically localized to specific limbs or chassis compartments.
  • Auxiliary Slots: Generic overflow or backup slots. These are highly modular spaces used to house secondary power cells, supplemental processing units, or redundant systems when primary slots are full.

The Assembly Process

Building a fully operational droid follows a strict, phase-by-step sequence to ensure all hardware and software components are structurally compatible.

Phase 1: The Structural Shell

The assembly begins with defining the droid’s size, load-bearing framework, and structural limits.

  • Chassis Selection: The base chassis dictates the core frame size, baseline Hit Points, baseline Strength, and total module capacity. It acts as the skeleton but starts completely hollow, providing only a structural shell -- hollow of modules, not of protection. Each chassis carries its own Damage Resistance, listed in its row, and that figure is the droid's body DR at the Torso: DR 5 for a Sentinel frame up to DR 20 for a heavy Quadrupedal one. Heads and Legs carry their own DR at their own locations. A utilized chassis does not add weight to a droid’s inventory carrying capacity.
  • The Power Core Requirement: The chassis must be fitted with an appropriate Power Core into its dedicated slot before any component can function. Without a power core, the droid is an inert pile of metal.

Phase 2: Assembling the Physical Anatomy

You must explicitly install the individual physical body parts. A droid only possesses the hit locations, reach limits, and manual dexterity of the specific appendages attached during this phase.

  • Head Installation: If the design calls for a centralized sensory center, a dedicated head must be mounted. This opens up the “Head” and “Face” hit locations and creates the housing for processors and primary sensors.
  • Arms: Defining manipulating limbs establishes the baseline reach and the ability to wield weapons or tools.
  • Manipulators: Attached to the arms to dictate fine manual dexterity or heavy-duty lifting capabilities.
  • Motive Struts: Attached to the lower (or upper in some cases) chassis to determine things like Lifting ST, Movement Speed, Jumping ability, and type of locomotion (bipedal, quadrupedal, etc).
  • Motive Mount: Attached to the Motive Struts (or chassis in some cases) to determine things like type of movement (Foot, hovering, tracked, or wheeled). Assists in making up the droids lifting, towing, and general movement abilities.

Phase 3: Hardware Integration

With the physical shell assembled, hardware upgrades and modifications are assigned to the specific body parts that house them.

  • Processor and Memory Core: The processor and memory core constitutes the “brain” of the droid. The Processor determines the baseline Intelligence, Will, and Perception. While the Memory Core houses the skills and memories of the droid. The Memory Core is first attached to the Processor, then they are installed together into the head unit.
  • Primary Sensors: The eyes/ears (Primary Sensors) are integrated directly into the Head housing.
  • Kinetic & Motor Integration: Upgrades are slotted into the Actuator and Reflex Wiring slots to establish the droid’s final Dexterity, Strength, and mechanical limits.
  • Core Upgrades: Fundamental enhancements, such as improved skeletal lacing, are applied to upgrade the baseline stats provided by the chassis.
  • Internal & External Slot Allocation: Modifications are distributed inside (Internal) or bolted outside (External) specific body parts.
  • Utility & Auxiliary Loadout: Built-in tools are mounted into Utility slots, while backup batteries or extra systems are assigned to Auxiliary slots.

Phase 4: System Calibrations and Final Boot

Once all parts are physically integrated, the lead engineer must initiate the System Calibration process.

  • Boot Sequence: The technician powers up the core and runs a diagnostic routine. A successful calibration boots the software parameters, maps the mechanical limbs to the processor, and brings the unit online as a fully functional character.

Installation, Modification, and Repair Mechanics

Whether building a droid from scratch, upgrading systems, or patching combat damage, the mechanical realities of the workshop dictate success.

Initial Construction (PCs vs. NPCs)
  • Player Character Droids: Player droids do not need to roll for their initial construction. Because these components and abilities are purchased with Character Points during character creation, the initial assembly is assumed to be a complete success.
  • NPC Droids: When an NPC droid is being assembled in-game, the assembler must roll to successfully install each individual part.
Skill Checks, Penalties, and Failure
  • Main Components: Installing core structural pieces requires an Engineer (Droids) or Robotics skill check. A character may substitute Mechanic (Droids), but rolls at a disadvantage.
  • Modifications and Upgrades: When simply adding modifications to an existing frame, Engineer (Droids) remains ideal, but Mechanic (Droids) can be used at no disadvantage. In a desperate pinch, a character can attempt to install modifications using Electronics Repair, but suffers a significant disadvantage.

Workshops, Tools, and Self-Repair

Once the campaign begins, any PC droid seeking new parts, modifications, or structural repairs must seek out a mechanic or rely on a skilled party member.

  • Environmental Modifiers: Working in a proper workshop grants a +2 bonus to the skill check. Attempting repairs or installations with no spare parts imposes a -5 penalty. Attempting the work with no tools and no spare parts is a massive -8 penalty.
  • Self-Modification and Repair: A player droid can attempt to repair or modify themselves, but navigating their own internal architecture is a logistical nightmare.
  • With Proper Skills: If the droid possesses the relevant training (Engineer or Mechanic), they suffer a standard -4 awkwardness penalty for working on themselves without a proper vantage point or leverage.
  • Defaulting to Attributes: If the droid lacks the specific skills and is forced to default to a raw attribute check (like Dexterity or Intelligence), the process is incredibly hazardous. They suffer a severe -8 penalty to the default roll, reflecting the extreme danger of blindly tinkering with sensitive power relays and processors without the proper know-how.

Droid Modification Malfunction Table

In the GURPS system, all installation, modification, and repair attempts are resolved by rolling 3d6 against the mechanic’s effective skill (e.g., Engineer (Droids) or Mechanic (Droids)). How that 3d6 roll resolves dictates which of the tables below is used:

  • Failure: A 3d6 roll that is greater than the character’s effective skill, but not high enough to be a critical failure. When this occurs, roll 1d6 on the Ordinary Failure table.
  • Critical Failure: A 3d6 roll of 18 is always a critical failure. A roll of 17 is a critical failure if the effective skill is 15 or less. Additionally, any roll of 10 or more above the effective skill is a critical failure (Basic Set: Campaigns, p. 348). When this occurs, roll 1d6 on the Critical Failure table.
Failure

An ordinary failure represents a slipped hydrospanner, misaligned wiring, or an improperly seated power coupling.

Droid Body Parts

The foundation of the droid. A Chassis must be selected first. It provides the base slots that other body parts and upgrades plug into. Each section of parts has an assigned hit location that coordinates to the Droid Hit Locations master table. This allows each droid to have a structured, custom hit location for each unique build.

Note: Cybernetic parts are designed for organics and not compatible with droid anatomies.

Pricing: every component below prices the same way as Armor Pieces, Weapons, and Cybernetics (Chapters 11-14): Material Value = Weight × Cost/lb, then one multiplier for each phase the build needs, applied in order.

  • A component's market price is its material value ×2 for Phase 1, Mechanic (Droids) (IQ/Average), which shapes raw stock into a part.
  • Fitting that part into the finished assembly is Phase 2, Electronics Repair (Droids) (IQ/Average), a further ×2 on the running total.
  • A part whose firmware the crafter loads -- any Processor or Memory Core -- then takes Phase 3, Computer Programming (IQ/Hard), a further ×3, reaching ×12.

Only a Processor or a Memory Core does; sensors and reflex wiring carry burned-in factory firmware the crafter never flashes, so every other part in this chapter stops at ×4, and every price below is that arithmetic rather than an authored figure; see the Pricing Note under Droid Components for the full chain and a worked example.

CP Cost: CP Cost is a separate figure -- the part's build-point cost for assembling a droid character -- and where the part grants a real GURPS trait it also adds 20 CR per Character Point to the base before any phase is applied (@UUID[Compendium.shadowbase.handbook.JournalEntry.Skjt6Gqhhw8BiF1Y]{Chapter 10}'s Traits Have a Price).

Attributes: A droid's ST and HP are set by its chassis -- each chassis states its baseline the way a Processor states the IQ it runs at, replacing the default 10. DX and HT begin at 10. Its parts move the rest from there: limbs, servos, and motive systems add Lifting or Striking ST (never base ST), and wiring modules add DX. A given part's bonus applies once to the droid, no matter how many are installed -- four legs don't quadruple Lifting ST. A droid pays that part's CP Cost once as well, however many copies it installs -- since the bonus applies once, so does its cost; extra copies add only credits and weight. A part built to stack instead -- a second weapon, an added power reserve, an extra manipulator arm -- is charged per copy, because its effect is per copy. Striking ST works as the advantage does: it adds to the droid's ST for melee (thrust/swing) damage exactly as for a living character, and is never halved or reduced for being a droid. The DX-wiring modules:

  • Upgraded Motor Relays +1 DX
  • Combat-Reaction Wiring +2 DX
  • Assassin-Grade Neuro-web +3 DX

Perception and Will follow IQ as they do for organics unless a part says otherwise, which is what the Combat Matrix's +2 Per and +2 Will are added to. Base ST and HP come from the chassis, DX from wiring, and IQ from the Processor; a droid with no DX-wiring module simply has DX 10, and the skill levels in the templates below are priced against these figures on @UUID[Compendium.shadowbase.handbook.JournalEntry.aHFgSZUXNODEwQd2]{Chapter 3}'s table.

Frame Size and Size Modifier: A droid's height is the sum of its parts -- head + chassis torso + motive stance (the leg, strut, tread, or hover clearance that lifts the frame; a foot rides with its leg). Its Size Modifier then follows the same rule as any character (@UUID[Compendium.shadowbase.handbook.JournalEntry.fZowiGenjFSpf9el]{Chapter 2}): SM = 6 x log10(height in feet / 6 ft), plus the chassis's shape adjustment -- +2 for a sphere or box frame, +1 for an elongated (quadruped or vehicular) frame -- rounded to two decimals (@UUID[Compendium.shadowbase.handbook.JournalEntry.sM4JaeipflPpOZgw]{Chapter 13}). Each template below prints its derived height and SM. A (Custom) part names no fixed height, the same way it names no fixed stats -- the GM sets its contribution at approval, so a build using one takes a GM-assigned height rather than one summed from the parts. A repulsor motive part also states a Float height -- the operational altitude it holds the droid at in flight (head-high for most; a low skim for a ground-hugging utility unit). Float is positional only: it is not part of the height sum and does not affect the Size Modifier.

Two Processors: Where two Processors are fitted, the droid thinks with the better of them: it runs at the higher IQ, and the other's traits still apply. So the HK's Heuristic governs its IQ 12 while its Combat Matrix still supplies +2 Per, +2 Will, Combat Reflexes and Callous, and the Sentinel -- Basic Labor beside a Combat Matrix, both at IQ 8 -- is unaffected either way.

Governing IQ: A processor's IQ bracket is part of its CP only when that processor governs the droid. Basic Labor, Cognitive, and Heuristic print their IQ bracket inside their CP Cost because a droid fitting one of them almost always runs on it; the Combat Matrix prints its traits only (30), because it is usually fitted as a co-processor whose IQ 8 never applies. When a Combat Matrix is the droid's governing processor, add IQ 8 [-40] to the template.

Mathematically Inclined: A droid whose governing processor runs at IQ 11 or higher -- a Cognitive, Heuristic, or Analytical-grade brain -- is inherently mathematically inclined: it has Mathematical Ability (@UUID[Compendium.shadowbase.handbook.JournalEntry.2I6Edey1uD2bgyES]{Chapter 4}) at no CP cost. Rapid, flawless calculation is simply what a thinking-grade droid processor does; beyond the usual +2 to Mathematics, the GM may let it apply to targeting solutions, astrogation, and similar rapid-calculation rolls. A combat- or labor-grade brain governing at IQ 8 -- the Combat Matrix or Basic Labor -- does not qualify. Among the templates below, the GE3, HK, T3, Municipal Patrol, R-8009, S6, and G0-T0 have it inherently; the Mark I-IV assault series and the Sentinel do not.

Size Modifier: Size Modifier comes from the Chassis where one carries it -- the Municipal Patrol's Repulsor Chassis at SM -1 is the only chassis in this chapter that does -- and it scales weight and cost as it does everywhere else (@UUID[Compendium.shadowbase.handbook.JournalEntry.sM4JaeipflPpOZgw]{Chapter 13}), without touching any attribute. A chassis that names no SM is SM 0.

Chassis

Main Chassis, selected first. The central structural framework and primary housing of the unit. It defines the basic physical profile, baseline mass, and the exact number of modular hardpoints available for limbs and core systems.

Hit Location: Torso
  • Hits to a droid’s chassis that penetrate DR usually only carry a x2 multiplier. Despite the reduced multiplier, penetrating Torso hits still trigger Major Wound checks. Precision criticals rolled on the Torso/Chassis can allow the GM to rule that the attack bypassed outer armor and specifically pierced an Internal Slot, damaging a built-in generator, commlink, or vital system.

Processor

Plugs into the Head unit. The “brain” of the droid dictates its free will, skill limit, and base Intelligence. It can be augmented with reflex wiring to improve the droid’s physical reaction times.

The Head must be pierced, crushed, or otherwise compromised to land a hit on the processor.

Note: Once equipped, processor weight does not add weight to a droid’s inventory carry capacity.

Multiple Processors: A Head unit provides exactly 1 Processor slot by default -- a droid can only be built with a second processor (like HK-series assassin droids' signature Heuristic + Combat Matrix pairing) by installing Expanded Processor Housing first, which adds a second Processor slot (and its own required Memory Core). When multiple processors are installed, the droid runs at the higher of the two IQs -- the other processor's IQ does not add or stack -- while both processors' other traits and bonuses still apply; the droid's skill-learning capacity follows whichever installed processor is the most permissive.

Fully Modular: a blank Datacard (@UUID[Compendium.shadowbase.handbook.JournalEntry.Skjt6Gqhhw8BiF1Y]{Chapter 10}, 174 CR) is loaded with the target personality matrix at a Droid Programming Terminal -- the Dedicated Tech-Bay (+0) tier for droid work, a workspace rather than an item to buy (see Programming a Datacard, @UUID[Compendium.shadowbase.handbook.JournalEntry.Skjt6Gqhhw8BiF1Y]{Chapter 10}) -- then flashed into the chip — the same Chip + Datacard + Programming Fee arrangement as Neural Implants (@UUID[Compendium.shadowbase.handbook.JournalEntry.o2ZbGiux36xwNCw0]{Chapter 14}). The card is a construction tool throughout this book -- it reverts to blank once the flash succeeds and is reused, so its 174 CR is never part of the Processor's price. Belt and Shield firmware (@UUID[Compendium.shadowbase.handbook.JournalEntry.sM4JaeipflPpOZgw]{Chapter 13}) works identically. What the item pays for is the Programming Fee, never the medium; see @UUID[Compendium.shadowbase.handbook.JournalEntry.Skjt6Gqhhw8BiF1Y]{Chapter 10}'s Blueprints for the one case where the card is kept. Memory Cores use the same system.

A droid’s body can be damaged and rebuilt, but a destroyed Memory Core is true death for that droid’s consciousness, personality, skills, and memories. If a droid is rebuilt after a lost memory core, it is treated as an entirely new character and must relearn any skills it had. Memory Core

Housed securely within the skull, linked directly to the Processor. The Memory Core is a universally standard, it’s a no CP cost internal component. While the Processor dictates a droid’s raw processing speed and skill limit, the Memory Core is the metaphysical “soul” of the droid. It houses the droid’s true consciousness, its accumulated memories, its personality matrix, and all Character Points (CP) spent on mental attributes and skills.

Hit Location: Processor/ Memory Core

Because it is a delicate internal component, the Memory Core does not have its own HP or DR. Instead, its condition is dictated entirely by the structural integrity of the droid’s Head. As the Head takes damage, the Memory Core is subjected to the following Damage States:

  • State: Corrupted (Major Wound Trigger): If a single blow to the Head inflicts damage equal to or greater than 1/2 the droid’s total HP (triggering a Major Wound), the kinetic shock or energy surge scrambles the core’s data matrix. The droid suffers a persistent -2 penalty to all IQ, Perception, and Will-based rolls until the core is repaired using Electronics Repair (Computers).
  • State: Destroyed (Massive Damage Trigger): If a single blow to the Head inflicts damage equal to or greater than the droid’s Total HP in one hit, the cranial housing is physically crushed, shattering the Memory Core.
  • State: Destroyed (Precision Critical Trigger): If an attacker rolls a 17 or 18 (Catastrophic Headshot) on the Critical Head & Face Blow Table, the attack pierces the processor and perfectly obliterates the core, bypassing the need for massive structural damage.
  • The Consequence of Destruction (True Death): If the Memory Core is Destroyed, the droid experiences True Death. Its consciousness, personality, and memories are permanently wiped. Even if a brand new memory core is installed into the repaired chassis, the droid is treated as a completely new Level 0 character that must relearn all skills.

Shield Projector. The Shield Projector is an activated deflector field, not passive plating. While switched on it projects a Force Field of DR 20 vs. energy around the entire chassis -- every hit location -- stacking on top of the droid's chassis and plating DR against energy attacks (blaster, ion, and other energy damage). Kinetic and physical attacks (slugs, melee, vibro-weapons, crushing) pass through it and meet the chassis and plating DR alone.

Power: the field draws on the power core at 3 PP per minute while active -- about 33 minutes on a standard 100 PP core, scaling with core upgrades (about 50 minutes at 150 PP, 83 at 250, 167 at 500), and running concurrently with the droid's 1 PP/minute combat draw. At 0 PP the field collapses.

Under fire: the field degrades exactly as armor and shields do (@UUID[Compendium.shadowbase.handbook.JournalEntry.JJ04T5LHImjlILs1]{Chapter 7}: Armor and Clothing Degradation). Each time an energy hit penetrates -- its damage exceeds the droid's total DR including the field, and the droid takes HP -- the field's current DR drops by 1, cumulative, until repaired; a Major Wound to a covered location drops it a full condition step. A hit the field fully absorbs does not erode it. At DR 0 the field is down until the emitter is repaired (Electronics Repair).

The emitter: the projector itself is a powered utility device on the External hardpoint -- Damaged, it runs the field at -1 DR to its output; Broken, the field drops entirely until repaired (@UUID[Compendium.shadowbase.handbook.JournalEntry.JJ04T5LHImjlILs1]{Chapter 7}).

Cost: the module is 50 CP -- half of an unlimited DR 20 (100 CP at 5 CP per level) -- the discount reflecting that it stops energy only and must be powered to run, in exchange for covering every location.

Crafting Droid Body Parts

Pricing Note: A droid component's price is its material value marked up once for every phase its construction needs, plus 20 CR per Character Point of any real GURPS trait it grants (@UUID[Compendium.shadowbase.handbook.JournalEntry.Skjt6Gqhhw8BiF1Y]{Chapter 10}'s Traits Have a Price). Use the CP magnitude -- a negative-CP part still adds 20 CR per point of |CP|, since complexity costs either way.

Structural Parts: A structural part takes two phases: ×2 for Phase 1, Mechanic (Droids) or Armoury (Cybernetics) -- both IQ/Average, so the choice never moves the price -- shaping raw material into a part, then ×2 again for Phase 2, Electronics Repair (Droids) (IQ/Average), wiring and fitting that part into the assembly.

Armor Plating: Armor plating has nothing to wire, so Phase 2 never applies to it as circuitry -- but a plate still has to be forged and fitted, and that is where the two rates in the plating table come from.

  • Plating built on Durasteel -- the Medium and Heavy plates, and the Cortosis and Beskar facings laid over a Durasteel backing -- is shaped in Phase 1 and fitted to the frame in Phase 2, reaching ×4.
  • Plating that is simply bolted on -- welded scrap panels, moulded Plastoid composite -- takes Phase 1 alone and stops at ×2.

Read it off the Construction column: if Durasteel is in the recipe the plate is forged, and it is ×4.

Firmware: A part whose firmware the crafter loads from a Datacard -- a Processor or Memory Core -- adds Phase 3, Computer Programming (IQ/Hard), at ×3, reaching ×12. Burned-in factory firmware (Sensors, reflex wiring) is not flashed by the crafter and takes no Phase 3. That firmware Datacard -- the personality matrix or core program -- is a separate card from the part’s Blueprint (@UUID[Compendium.shadowbase.handbook.JournalEntry.Skjt6Gqhhw8BiF1Y]{Chapter 10}): building a Processor or Memory Core needs both in hand.

Worked: a Motion Sensor is 38 CR of materials plus 10 CP of Detect at 20 CR each = 238 base; 238 × 2 = 476 for Phase 1; 476 × 2 = 952 for Phase 2.

Building from a Blueprint: Every item you build -- whether it appears in this chapter’s tables or not -- requires its Blueprint in hand (@UUID[Compendium.shadowbase.handbook.JournalEntry.Skjt6Gqhhw8BiF1Y]{Chapter 10}: Blueprints): buy the plan for a catalog item, reverse-engineer it from a Deconstruction, or author an original through the Design Phase. Owning or knowing of an item is not knowing how to make one. A proven plan builds at the baseline; a degraded copy or an unproven original takes its penalty on every Crafting Phase roll below.

Building a droid’s chassis and appendages requires precision metallurgy combined with complex neurological mapping.

Skills Required:
  • Physical Hardware (Chassis, Arms, Motive Struts): Armoury (Cybernetics) or Mechanic (Droids) to smelt, shape, and assemble the durasteel framework and synthetic myomer musculature.
  • Electronics & Processors (Head, Sensors, Power Core): Electronics Repair (Droids) to wire the optic relays, logic gates, and primary energy distribution networks.
  • Software Initialization: Any functional body part with an electronic component requires a Computer Programming roll to sync the local drivers with the droid’s primary Processor.
Base Time:
  • Hardware Assembly: 1 hour of continuous labor per pound of the final scaled weight.
  • Software Initialization: 1 hour of coding and driver calibration per distinct body part.
Workspace Modifiers:
  • Improvised/Field Tools (-5 to skill): Using a standard hydrospanner and pocket multi-tools in the dirt.
  • Basic Toolkit (-2 to skill): Using a portable robotics repair kit in a safe environment.
  • Dedicated Tech-Bay (+0 to skill): A facility equipped with diagnostics, proper ventilation, and static-free zones.
  • Advanced Droid Foundry (+2 to skill): Industrial manufacturing bays like those of Cybot Galactica or Industrial Automaton.
  • Taking Extra Time: As @UUID[Compendium.shadowbase.handbook.JournalEntry.Skjt6Gqhhw8BiF1Y]{Chapter 10} (General Gear & Currency): double the base time for +1, four times for +2, eight times for +3, fifteen times for +4, thirty times for +5, whatever your tools.

Default appearance. A droid part with no finish specified looks like the material it is made of: Durasteel dull gunmetal gray; Plasteel off-white with a faint sheen; Plastoid bone white; Scrap Metal mismatched, rusted and pitted; Beskar bright polished silver; Aurodium rich yellow gold. A droid assembled from several materials shows its Chassis finish unless the owner says otherwise.

Coloring: Paint and plating are free and change nothing — no weight, no cost, no DR, no function. A builder working at a Dedicated Tech-Bay or Advanced Droid Foundry simply declares a droid's color scheme, markings and finish, with no roll and no extra time: astromech livery, corporate house colors, military drab, a battered scavenger's patchwork. Improvised/Field Tools and a Basic Toolkit can assemble the part but not finish it, and it comes out the default shade of its material. The same applies to repainting a droid already built — which is why a droid that changes hands often changes colors with it.

Failure Conditions:
  • Hardware Failure: A failed roll ruins the structural integrity of the chassis or appendage. 50% of the raw materials are wasted and must be replaced. A critical failure destroys 100% of the materials and may cause a localized power short (1d-3 electrical damage to the crafter).
  • Software Failure: The body part is physically sound but “bricked.” It fails to communicate with the main Processor. No materials are wasted, but the crafter must spend an additional hour debugging the firmware before rolling again.

Swapping Firmware in an Installed Processor

  • While the Processor remains installed, its personality matrix can be replaced without pulling the physical chip: load a blank Datacard with the new matrix and flash it through the Processor's external port. Sensors cannot use this process, since their firmware is burned in at the factory rather than flashed from a card.
  • Skills Required: Computer Operation to flash the new matrix through the Processor's external port.
  • Base Time: 10 minutes of syncing and biometric re-calibration.
  • Success: The Processor now runs the new matrix; the old one is overwritten. The Datacard used for the flash reverts to blank and is reused, exactly as after a fresh Crafting installation.
  • Failure: A minor installation glitch or biometric mismatch. The installer wastes 10 minutes and must attempt the roll again.
  • Critical Failure: The mismatch corrupts both the incoming and the chip’s prior calibration data. The Processor is non-functional until a full Computer Programming roll re-establishes it, per Crafting.

Swapping Droid Body Parts

  • Replacing one body part with another in a single operation -- a burnt-out Optic for a fresh one, a Bipedal Leg for a Tread Assembly, a Standard Arm for a Heavy Lifting Arm. Distinct from Uninstalling followed by a separate installation: the droid is powered down once rather than twice, and the chassis mounting is never left open. Unlike cybernetics, no surgery is involved -- a droid is hardware throughout, and a technician needs a workshop rather than an operating theatre.
  • Skills Required: Mechanic (Droids) for the physical work, plus Electronics Repair (Droids) where the part carries firmware. Base Time: 30 minutes per part swapped. Workspace Modifiers and the Droid Modification Malfunction Table apply as for any other modification. Success: the old part comes out intact at its established value and the new one seats cleanly. Failure: the new part is misaligned -- the hit location it governs is non-functional until another 30 minutes of realignment. Critical Failure: roll on the Droid Modification Malfunction Table. A powered-down droid takes no rejection risk; swapping parts on an active droid is at -4.

Uninstalling Droid Body Parts

  • Preserves the part as an intact, reusable component instead of reducing it to scrap -- the reliable version of the rare bonus that Salvaging’s critical success sometimes grants.
  • Skills Required: Mechanic (Droids) for physical limbs/chassis; Electronics Repair (Droids) for heads and processors.
  • Base Time: 45 minutes of labor per pound of total weight -- between Crafting’s full hour of assembly and Salvaging’s half hour of teardown.
  • Sensors and Reflex Wiring: Their firmware is burned in at the factory (see Sensors, above), so an intact extraction recovers working hardware, not a swappable trait -- reinstalling it elsewhere grants that same fixed sensory effect to the new mount.
  • Processors and Memory Cores: This is the intended way to “rescue” a droid’s mind from a dying or obsolete chassis -- a successful Deconstruction preserves the personality matrix and memories exactly as they were, ready to be installed in a new Head/Processor housing.
  • Success: The part is extracted fully intact and functional, retaining its established Base/Market Cost value from its component table, ready to install on a compatible chassis.
  • Critical Success: As above, plus 25% of the surrounding casing’s raw material weight is recovered too.
  • Failure: The part is ruined; it’s only good for Salvaging’s raw-material yield, not reuse.
  • Critical Failure: The part is destroyed outright. For a Processor or Memory Core, this risks the same neural-pathway brick described under Salvaging -- and for a Memory Core specifically, this is the True Death condition described above.

Deconstructing Droid Body Parts

  • While Salvaging reduces a body part to one blended raw-material yield, Deconstruction recovers each distinct material separately at a better rate -- a Chassis built from both Durasteel and Silicon yields each material on its own instead of one averaged pool.

Recording a Blueprint: A successful Deconstruction is also the moment to record a Blueprint of the part (@UUID[Compendium.shadowbase.handbook.JournalEntry.Skjt6Gqhhw8BiF1Y]{Chapter 10}: Blueprints) -- a blank Datacard and a Computer Operation roll, made during the teardown. Salvaging never yields one.

  • Skills Required: The same skill Salvaging would use for that part’s category (Mechanic (Droids) for physical limbs/chassis; Electronics Repair (Droids) for heads and processors).
  • Base Time: 60 minutes of labor per pound of total weight -- twice Salvaging's 30, and about as long as assembling the part in the first place, since carefully reversing a build is much the same work in reverse.
  • Success: Recover 75% of each distinct material's raw weight, separately, rather than one blended 50%, and any finished sub-component built into the part -- a Power Cell, a Memory Core -- comes out whole at its listed price instead of being reduced to material at all.
  • Critical Success: 90% of each material, separately, and every sub-component survives whole.
  • Failure / Critical Failure: The same consequences as Salvaging, below -- the attempt is still a delicate teardown, just aimed at precision instead of speed.

Salvaging Droid Body Parts

Dismantling a destroyed or obsolete droid yields valuable raw materials and occasionally intact sub-components.

  • Skills Required: Mechanic (Droids) for physical limbs/chassis; Electronics Repair (Droids) for heads and processors.

  • Failure Conditions: A failed physical roll warps the casing, reducing it to low-value scrap. A failed electronic roll bricks the neural pathways, rendering any recovered processors useless.

Crafting & Installing Droid Upgrades

Upgrades alter a droid’s internal core functionality or bolt onto external hardpoints. They require balancing structural integrity with the delicate tuning of the droid’s existing power grid.

Building from a Blueprint: Every item you build -- in the tables above or not -- requires its Blueprint in hand (@UUID[Compendium.shadowbase.handbook.JournalEntry.Skjt6Gqhhw8BiF1Y]{Chapter 10}: Blueprints): buy it, reverse-engineer it from a Deconstruction, or author an original. A proven plan builds at the baseline; a degraded copy or an unproven original takes its penalty on every phase roll below.

Skills Required:
  • Fabrication: Engineer (Droids) or Armoury (depending on the specific upgrade) to build the part from scratch.
  • Installation (Physical): Mechanic (Droids) to physically mount actuators, armor plating, or auxiliary batteries.
  • Installation (Software): Computer Programming to write the proprietary code that translates the new hardware to the droid’s operating system.
Base Time & Workspace:
  • Physical Installation: 30 minutes of careful labor per upgrade slot occupied.
  • Firmware Calibration: 1 hour of system handshake testing and biometric synchronization.
  • Workspace modifiers apply identically to Droid Body Parts.
Failure Consequences:
  • Installation Failure: The upgrade is improperly seated or the mounting rails are warped. The modification is non-functional, and the installer must spend another 30 minutes realigning it. A critical failure damages the host body part, reducing its DR by 1 until repaired.
  • Software Failure: The “Ghost Glitch.” The upgrade is physically secure, but the firmware refuses to sync. The installer must spend 30 minutes debugging. A critical failure bricks the upgrade entirely, requiring a full rebuild.

Uninstalling Droid Upgrades

  • Safely detaching an upgrade so it can be reused on a different chassis, rather than salvaging it for raw materials.
  • Skills Required: Mechanic (Droids).
  • Base Time: 15 minutes of labor per slot occupied.
  • Success: The upgrade is detached intact and ready to be mounted on a different chassis.
  • Failure: The mounting brackets shear. The upgrade survives but requires a successful repair roll before it can be reinstalled anywhere.
  • Critical Failure: The component is destroyed outright.

Deconstructing Droid Upgrades

  • While Salvaging reduces an upgrade to one blended raw-material yield, Deconstruction recovers each distinct material separately at a better rate -- Beskar Alloy plating built from both Beskar and Durasteel yields each material on its own instead of one averaged pool.

Recording a Blueprint: A successful Deconstruction can also record a Blueprint of the upgrade (@UUID[Compendium.shadowbase.handbook.JournalEntry.Skjt6Gqhhw8BiF1Y]{Chapter 10}: Blueprints) -- a blank Datacard and a Computer Operation roll. Salvaging never yields one.

  • Skills Required: Engineer (Droids) or Armoury for physical components; Electronics Repair (Droids) for anything with functional circuitry.
  • Base Time: 30 minutes of labor per pound of the upgrade’s total weight -- twice Salvaging’s time, in exchange for material-by-material precision.
  • Success: Recover 50% of each distinct material’s raw weight, separately, rather than one blended total.
  • Critical Success: 75% of each material.
  • Failure / Critical Failure: The same consequences as Salvaging, above -- the attempt is still a delicate teardown, just aimed at precision instead of speed.

Salvaging Droid Upgrades

  • Breaking down a damaged, obsolete, or unwanted upgrade to reclaim its raw materials, rather than preserving it for reuse.
  • Skills Required: Engineer (Droids) or Armoury for physical components; Electronics Repair (Droids) for anything with functional circuitry.
  • Base Time: 15 minutes of labor per pound of the upgrade’s total weight.
  • Yield Rates: Standard Success: Recover 50% of the raw material weight. Critical Success: Recover 75% of the raw material weight.
  • Failure Conditions: A failed Engineer (Droids) or Armoury roll reduces the raw materials to low-value scrap. A failed Electronics Repair roll destroys any circuitry entirely -- no materials are recovered from that portion of the upgrade.

Droid Damage Conditions

Characters with fully robotic bodies react differently to damage than flesh and blood. Lacking a traditional nervous system and blood vessels, they ignore several organic vulnerabilities but introduce unique mechanical risks.

I. No Shock Penalties and Major Wounds Damage to a mechanical limb or a droid chassis does not inflict a Shock Penalty, as mechanical constructs do not feel pain. However, they are still vulnerable to sudden, massive trauma representing structural shock or system disruption.

  • Major Wounds: If a droid character takes damage in a single blow equal to or greater than half their total HP, they suffer a Major Wound. They must immediately roll against HT to avoid stunning or shutdown, just as organics do to avoid unconsciousness.
  • Malfunctions: The player must roll on the Droid Malfunction Table (@UUID[Compendium.shadowbase.handbook.JournalEntry.JJ04T5LHImjlILs1]{Chapter 7}). High rolls can result in a Core Overload, immediate loss of Power Points (PP), internal fires, or force an immediate HT-5 roll to avoid total shutdown, regardless of the initial damage multiplier.

II. Fluid Leaks and Power Drain Droids do not bleed blood. Instead, crippling strikes rupture fluid lines, lubricants, and coolant channels.

  • The Trigger: Whenever a mechanical limb or chassis suffers a Crippling Injury, the character must immediately make a HT roll. On a failure, they begin to leak.
  • The Drain: Instead of losing HP, the character loses 5 Power Points (PP) per interval. This represents the loss of vital fluids forcing the power core to work harder, leading to an accelerated shutdown rather than physical death. The interval is every 10 seconds in combat, or every 1 minute out of combat.
  • Stabilization: The leak stops naturally if the character achieves three consecutive successful HT rolls. Alternatively, it can be patched instantly with a successful Mechanic or Armoury roll and the appropriate tools.

III. Head and Processor Hits Droids rely on central processors rather than organic brain tissue.

  • Damage Multipliers: Hits to a droid’s “head” (if it has one) or main chassis that penetrate DR usually only carry a x2 multiplier (rather than the organic x4), unless specifically targeting a volatile component like a power core.
  • Wound Checks: Despite the reduced multiplier, penetrating head hits still trigger Major Wound checks.

IV. Crippling and Amputation Mechanical limbs are subject to the exact same crippling and amputation thresholds as organic limbs.

  • Limbs (Arms, Legs, Motive Struts): Crippled if the location takes damage over 1/2 HP in a single blow.
  • Extremities (Hands, Feet, Manipulators): Crippled if the location takes damage over 1/3 HP in a single blow.
  • Mechanical parts do not heal. A crippled mechanical limb or extremity is rendered “broken” and remains non-functional until repaired using the appropriate Engineer (Droids), Mechanic (Droids), Armoury (Cybernetics) skills.
  • Modifications: If a mechanical limb is crippled (takes over 1/2 HP), any modifications installed within that limb are temporarily disabled or jammed.
  • Repairs: A crippled or amputated mechanical limb requires mechanical repair (using skills like Mechanic or Armoury), to restore function.

V. Ionization and EMP Vulnerability Due to their electrical nature, droids are highly vulnerable to ion blasters, EMP grenades, and localized electrical surges.

  • When struck by a weapon with an Electrical Surge modifier, the mechanical target takes its standard damage.
  • Regardless of the damage penetrating DR, the target must immediately make a HT roll. On a failure, the droid is completely paralyzed or deactivated for a set duration (typically 1d minutes).

VI.Integrated Modifications: Installed modifications (e.g., hidden blasters, micro-jets, cyber-jacks) are not treated as separate, targetable hit locations. Equipment is considered integrated into the body part that houses it.

  • Crippling Hits: If a mechanical limb is crippled (takes over 1/2 HP), any modifications installed within that limb are temporarily disabled or jammed.
  • Destruction: If a body part takes twice the HP needed to cripple it, or drops to negative HP, the limb is completely destroyed. All modifications housed within it are permanently destroyed.
  • Precision Criticals: If an attacker rolls a Critical Hit on a droid’s Torso/Chassis, the GM may rule that the attack bypassed outer armor and specifically pierced an Internal Slot, damaging a built-in modification, tool, or vital system.

Organic characters typically spend earned Character Points (CP) over time to “work out” and naturally increase their physical Strength (ST) or Dexterity (DX). Droids cannot do this. A droid’s physical attributes do not improve organically over time.

Instead, droid progression in the campaign is split into two distinct economies: Software (CP) and Hardware (CR).

Software Updates (Using CP)

Droids use earned Character Points exclusively to upgrade their programming. A droid player may spend CP on:

  • Mental Attributes: Increasing IQ, Perception (Per), or Willpower (Will).
  • Skills: Purchasing new skills or raising existing ones represents compiling heuristic learning or downloading a new skill matrix.
  • Mental Advantages: Purchasing traits like Language Talent, Absolute Timing, or Combat Reflexes.

Hardware Upgrades (Using CR)

To improve physical combat capabilities, a droid must rely entirely on hardware augmentation. If a droid wishes to increase its Strength (ST), Dexterity (DX), Movement (Move), or Damage Resistance (DR), it must purchase physical upgrades using Credits (CR) or scavenge parts from fallen enemies.

Once the parts are acquired, the droid must undergo maintenance by an organic companion (or another droid) with the Mechanic (Droids) skill to install the new servos, actuators, or armor plating.

Example Droid Templates

While balancing biological species to 0 CP is a great way to ensure all organic players start on an even playing field, applying that same rule to droids will break the point-buy balance inherent to them. If a campaign starts at 150 CP, an organic player starts with 150 points to spend. If the HK Droid is also treated as a “free” 0 CP species, that player effectively starts the game with 446 points worth of abilities (296 from the free template + 150 starting points). They will completely outshine the organic players in every encounter.

The Rule: So a droid character pays for its template out of the campaign's starting Character Points, exactly as an organic pays for attributes and advantages out of theirs -- the chassis is not a free species. Add up the Baseline, each distinct component's CP Cost (counted once per part -- see Attributes, above), the Additional Traits and the Skills; that sum is what the droid costs, and what remains is what the player has left to spend.
